title: Strategy Before and After the Flop
intro: This page turns the arithmetic into a way of playing no-limit hold'em: which hands to play from each seat, how to raise and re-raise before the flop, what to do on the flop, turn and river, how to size bets, and how to read opponents from their actions and statistics. The numbers given are typical of a six-handed cash game with 100 big blind stacks; they move with the table, the stacks and the opponents.

blocks.text: Why position matters

Acting last is an advantage on every street. The player in position sees whether the opponent checks or bets before choosing, can take a free card by checking behind, can control the size of the pot, and gets to see more of the opponent's actions before each decision. Because of that, a hand earns more in position than out of it; the same hand can be a raise on the button and a fold under the gun. The blinds lose money for everyone, mainly because they must put money in without seeing their cards, and also because after the flop they are out of position against everyone except each other.
Preflop: opening ranges

With rare exceptions, enter a pot by raising (opening), not by calling. A raise can win the blinds at once, takes the initiative, and makes the pot bigger when your hand is better than the ranges that call. Typical open sizes online are 2 to 2.5 big blinds, larger in live games and from the small blind. Players widen their opening range as their position gets later, because fewer players remain behind them who could hold a better hand:

blocks.source:
Seat (6-max)   Rough share of hands opened   Example of the weakest opens
UTG / LJ       15 - 18%                      77, A2s-A5s, KTs, QJs, AJo, KQo
HJ             19 - 22%                      55, K9s, T9s, 98s, ATo, KJo
CO             25 - 30%                      33, A2s, K7s, 87s, A9o, QJo
BTN            40 - 50%                      22, K2s, 64s, A2o, K9o, JTo
SB             35 - 45% (raise or limp)      varies widely with the strategy

blocks.text: Ranges like these come from solver studies and differ from one source to another by a few percent; what matters is the shape. Early opens are mostly pairs, strong aces and broadway cards. Late opens add suited hands of all kinds, which make flushes and straights and play well after the flop, and weaker offsuit hands.
Preflop: 3-bets, 4-bets and squeezes

items: 3-bet: a re-raise of an open, typically to about 3 times the open in position and 4 times out of position. A 3-bet range has value hands (QQ+, AK, and more against a wide opener) and some bluffs. Good 3-bet bluffs are hands that block the opener's continuing range and play well if called: suited aces such as A5s (the ace blocks AA and AK, and the hand makes nut flushes and wheels) and suited broadways.

Linear and polarised 3-betting: a linear (merged) 3-bet range is the top hands down to a cut-off, used against opponents who call 3-bets too much. A polarised one is the top hands plus some bluffs, with the medium hands flatted (just called), used when the opener folds or 4-bets a lot.

4-bet: a raise of a 3-bet, usually to about 2.2 to 2.5 times the 3-bet. With 100 bb stacks this often means committing to the pot, so 4-bet ranges are narrow: very strong hands, plus bluffs that block them (Ax, especially A5s).
Squeeze: a 3-bet after an open and one or more callers. The callers have shown hands too weak to 3-bet themselves (their ranges are capped), so a squeeze often wins the pot at once.
Cold call: calling a raise when you have no money in the pot yet. Calling a 3-bet or open in the big blind is easier, because you already have a big blind in and close the action.

blocks.text: The big blind defends very wide against a small open, because the pot odds are good: against a 2.5 bb open from the button, calling 1.5 bb more makes a final pot of 5.5 bb, so it needs only about 27% equity before thinking about position. Against small opens, strong players defend half or more of their hands from the big blind.
Postflop: board texture

Before acting on the flop, ask which range the board favours. A dry board, such as K 7 2 of three suits, has few draws and changes little on later streets. A wet (dynamic) board, such as J T 8 with two hearts, connects with many hands and gives many draws, so the best hand on the flop often isn't the best by the river. Boards also differ in which player's range they hit:

items: High boards with an ace or king favour the preflop raiser, whose range has more strong aces and kings.
Low and middle connected boards, such as 7 6 5, favour the caller, especially a big blind who defended with many small suited hands and pairs.
Paired boards and monotone boards (three cards of one suit) change which hands are strong and are usually played with small bets or checks.
Range advantage is having more equity across your whole range; nut advantage is having more of the very strongest hands. They decide how often and how big to bet, see #/poker/game-theory.

blocks.text: Postflop: betting lines

items: Continuation bet (c-bet): a bet on the flop by the player who raised last before it. On boards that favour the raiser's range, a small c-bet (a quarter to a third of the pot) with most of the range is common; on boards that favour the caller, the raiser checks more and bets bigger with a narrower range.
Check-raise: checking, then raising after the opponent bets. A strong weapon out of position, used with very strong hands and with draws as semi-bluffs.
Donk bet (lead): betting into the previous street's aggressor from out of position. Once seen as a mistake, it is now used on boards that favour the caller's range.
Float: calling a bet in position with a weak hand, planning to take the pot later when the opponent shows weakness.
Probe bet: betting the turn out of position after the aggressor checked behind on the flop.
Delayed c-bet: the raiser checks the flop and bets the turn.
Barrel: betting again on the next street after betting this one; a triple barrel bets flop, turn and river.
Slowplay (trapping): checking or calling with a very strong hand to keep weaker hands in or induce bluffs.
Pot control: checking a medium-strength hand to keep the pot small, so you aren't bet off it or forced to call a big river bet.
Overbet: a bet bigger than the pot. Used with a polarised range when you hold more of the nuts, see #/poker/game-theory.

blocks.text: Value bets and bluffs

A bet is for value when worse hands call it; it is a bluff when better hands fold to it. A bet that does neither, that only gets called by better hands and only folds worse ones, is a bad bet. A thin value bet is one with a hand that is only a little ahead of the calling range: the river bet with top pair, weak kicker, against an opponent who calls with second pair. Good bluffs on the river are hands with no showdown value that block the opponent's calling hands and don't block their folding hands.

Sizing follows the range. Bigger bets want more polarised ranges (very strong hands and bluffs); smaller bets suit wider ranges with many medium hands. Sizing to get all-in by the river is called geometric sizing: if the pot is $P$ and the stack is $S$, betting the same fraction $f$ of the pot on each of $n$ streets gets the stack in when

blocks.caption: With a pot of 10 bb and stacks of 95 bb, three streets of about 86% of the pot get all the money in.

blocks.text: Reading opponents

Exploitative play adjusts to an opponent's mistakes: bluffing more against a player who folds too much, value-betting thinner against one who calls too much, and folding more against one who never bluffs. It earns more than balanced play against weak opponents, but opens you to counter-adjustment by strong ones. Common player types:

items: Tight-aggressive (TAG): plays few hands, mostly by raising. The winning style for most players.
Loose-aggressive (LAG): plays many hands, aggressively. Hard to play against when done well, expensive when not.
Nit (rock): plays very few hands and rarely bluffs. Bluff them often; fold to their raises.
Calling station: calls too much and rarely raises. Value-bet thinly and never bluff them.
Maniac: bets and raises with almost anything. Call down wider and let them bluff.

Fish (recreational player): a weak, usually loose-passive player. Games are profitable because of them; game selection, choosing the games with the weakest opponents, is one of the biggest sources of a professional's win rate.

blocks.text: Online players track opponents with a heads-up display (HUD) of statistics from past hands, and live players keep the same ideas in their heads:

items: VPIP (voluntarily put money in pot): the share of hands in which a player calls or raises preflop, not counting the blinds they are forced to post. A winning six-handed regular is around 22 to 28%; above 40% is very loose.
PFR (preflop raise): the share of hands they raise preflop. A big gap between VPIP and PFR means they call a lot.
3-bet %: how often they 3-bet when they have the chance.
Fold to 3-bet, fold to c-bet: how often they give up against aggression.
C-bet %: how often they continuation-bet the flop.

AF (aggression factor): bets plus raises divided by calls, after the flop. WTSD (went to showdown) and W\$SD (won money at showdown) show how often they go to showdown and how often they win when they do.
Sample size matters: VPIP settles within a few dozen hands, a river statistic may need thousands. Read every number with the number of chances behind it.

blocks.text: Live players also watch tells: physical or behavioural signs of hand strength, such as how fast someone acts, how they stack chips or how their posture changes. Timing tells (how long a player takes) exist online too. Tells are most useful from weak players, who don't think about hiding them.
The mental game

items: Tilt: playing worse because of emotion, usually after a bad beat (losing a hand you were a big favourite to win) or a run of losses. The most expensive leak most players have. Stop playing when it shows.
Results-oriented thinking: judging decisions by their outcomes. Review hands by their EV, not by whether you won.
Leveling: guessing what the opponent thinks you think. Useful against thinking players, wasted on ones who play their own cards.

blocks.title: Big blind defence
blocks.text: Everyone folds to the button, who raises to 2.5 bb. The small blind folds. You are in the big blind. What equity do you need to call, ignoring what happens after the flop?
blocks.hint: Work out what you must add and the total pot after your call. The blinds (0.5 + 1) are already in.
solution: The pot holds 2.5 (button) + 0.5 (small blind) + 1 (your big blind) = 4 bb. You call 1.5 bb more, making 5.5 bb.
Required equity $= 1.5 / 5.5 \approx 27\%$. Many hands have that much against a button range, which is why the big blind defends so wide, though out of position it realises less than its full equity.

blocks.title: Geometric sizing
blocks.text: The pot on the flop is 6 bb and the effective stacks are 50 bb. What constant fraction of the pot, bet on the flop, turn and river, gets the stacks all in on the river?
solution: $f = (2.605 - 1)/2 \approx 0.80$: about 80% of the pot on each street. Check: 6 to 15.6 to 40.7 to about 106 bb, which is the 6 bb pot plus 50 bb from each player.
blocks.answer: about 80% of the pot each street
